Storm reviews: the strongest lows, one at a time

← Back to the archive
ERA5 proxy, not direct observation. Every storm here was found in ERA5 reanalysis by the project's pipeline A tracker, and every chart is drawn from ERA5 fields (0.25°, 6-hourly). 5 of the ten are before the 2004–05 season, where no archive record exists; the other 5 are since then, and are still read here from ERA5. ERA5 smooths the very strongest winds and pressure minima, so real peaks may be stronger. These are case studies, not a trend: nothing here says whether such storms are becoming more or less common.

North Atlantic

The five deepest North Atlantic storms

North Atlantic, 15 December 1986

Rank 1 by lowest ERA5 central pressure in the North Atlantic. ERA5 proxy, pipeline A track 72089.
In plain words

ERA5 puts its lowest pressure at 912.3 hPa on 15 Dec 1986 0000Z, near 59.8°N 34.8°W. Its fastest 24 h fall was 53 hPa, ending 14 Dec 1986 1800Z at about 57°N (the bomb threshold there is 23 hPa, so it qualifies as a bomb by that yardstick). It first reached hurricane-force-equivalent gusts (index at least 71.7 kt) on 14 Dec 1986 1200Z near 58.5°N 35.0°W, was at that strength in 8 of its 6-hourly fixes (about 48 h from first to last), and peaked at a gust index of 102 kt on 15 Dec 1986 0600Z. The gust swath maximum anywhere in the window, land included, is 102 kt.

Not direct observation. This storm is before the 2004–05 season. No archive record covers it, so every number and map here is ERA5 reanalysis. The gust index also runs high before 2001 (ERA5 gust drifts upward at fixed storm depth), so read its level with caution; central pressure is the better yardstick. No trend is drawn from it.

North Atlantic, 10 January 1993 — the Braer storm, 10-11 Jan 1993 (name inferred from date and position)

Rank 2 by lowest ERA5 central pressure in the North Atlantic. ERA5 proxy, pipeline A track 128894.
In plain words

ERA5 puts its lowest pressure at 914.9 hPa on 10 Jan 1993 1800Z, near 61.0°N 14.2°W. Its fastest 24 h fall was 64 hPa, ending 10 Jan 1993 1800Z at about 59°N (the bomb threshold there is 24 hPa, so it qualifies as a bomb by that yardstick). It first reached hurricane-force-equivalent gusts (index at least 71.7 kt) on 10 Jan 1993 0600Z near 59.2°N 20.2°W, was at that strength in 6 of its 6-hourly fixes (about 36 h from first to last), and peaked at a gust index of 108 kt on 10 Jan 1993 1800Z. The tracker only picks it up 24 h before the lowest pressure, so its early development, and the 24 h fall above, are only partly captured. The gust swath maximum anywhere in the window, land included, is 108 kt.

Method

How the storms were chosen and drawn

The ten storms are the five with the lowest ERA5 central pressure in each basin among the 1979–2025 tracks of pipeline A (the research tracker, research/era5/hf_history), with tropical-cyclone-flagged tracks left out. That removed two Pacific tracks (30 Oct 1989 and 3 Oct 1981) that would otherwise rank second and third. Ranking is by pressure alone, so the list is not a list of the strongest winds.

Central pressure, position and gust index come from the 6-hourly pipeline A fixes. The gust index is the highest ERA5 10 m gust over ocean within 800 km of the low. The weather maps use WeatherBench2 ERA5 at 0.25°, 6-hourly (sea-level pressure, 500 hPa geopotential height, 250 hPa wind speed), re-centred on the storm at each map time. The swath uses ERA5 hourly instantaneous gusts every 3 h over the 72 h window. The 24 h fall is the change in central pressure over the previous 24 h at each 6-hourly fix; the bomb line scales 24 hPa per 24 h at 60°N by sin(latitude)/sin(60°).

Read with care. ERA5 proxy throughout, never validated for storms before the archive begins. Before 2001 the gust index drifts upward at fixed storm depth, so gust numbers for the 1980s and 1990s storms are less reliable than their pressures. Not independently re-checked: how closely these ERA5 pressures match the observed minima of the named storms.

Seasons run 1 June to 31 May. Fields: WeatherBench2 ERA5 and ARCO-ERA5 (Google Cloud public data). Back to the archive
